title: Explain Basic Concepts Related to Artificial Intelligence (AI)

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: AI can generate, summarize, analyze, and automate, but its output is not automatically correct, private, unbiased, or appropriate. Understand integration, policy, limitations, and private-versus-public data concerns.
sections.callout: Integrate → use appropriately → verify output → protect data.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Recognize how AI integrates with applications, which policies govern it, why outputs require verification, and when data security or privacy changes the decision.

sections.title: Application Integration
paragraphs: AI may be built into productivity, search, help-desk, development, and business applications to generate, summarize, analyze, or assist inside a workflow.
sections.callout: Convenient integration does not remove security, authorization, accuracy, or policy requirements.

sections.title: Policy
paragraphs: Organizational, educational, legal, and business policies determine approved tools, allowed tasks, acceptable input data, and required human review.

sections.title: Appropriate Use
paragraphs: Before using AI, ask whether it is permitted for the task, with the data, in the environment. Do not send confidential records to a public service without authorization.

sections.title: Plagiarism
paragraphs: Presenting AI-generated material as original work may violate school, workplace, attribution, or task rules. AI assistance is not automatically plagiarism; use and policy determine the concern.

sections.title: Limitations
paragraphs: AI output must be evaluated rather than accepted as truth. The published limitations are bias, hallucinations, and accuracy.

sections.title: Bias
paragraphs: Bias is systematically skewed or unfair output caused by training data, selection, model behavior, or problem framing.

sections.title: Hallucinations
paragraphs: A hallucination is plausible-sounding but fabricated or incorrect information, such as nonexistent sources, commands, facts, or product features.

sections.title: Accuracy
paragraphs: AI output can be correct, partial, outdated, misleading, or wrong. Verify important technical and business facts with trustworthy sources.
sections.callout: Skewed → bias; made up → hallucination; correct? → accuracy.

sections.title: Private vs. Public AI

entries.title: Private
paragraphs: Provides greater organizational control over deployment and data handling but still requires security controls.

entries.title: Public
paragraphs: An external or shared service whose terms, data handling, privacy, security, and policy approval must be understood before sensitive use.

sections.callout: Before pasting, know where the data goes.

sections.title: Data Security
paragraphs: Protect AI inputs such as credentials, customer records, proprietary code, internal documents, and regulated data from unauthorized access, loss, or compromise.

sections.title: Data Source
paragraphs: The data source is where information originates. Outdated, incorrect, incomplete, or biased source data can degrade results.
sections.callout: Where did the information come from?

sections.title: Data Privacy
paragraphs: Privacy governs appropriate collection, access, use, sharing, and protection of personal or sensitive information.
sections.callout: Protect against compromise → security; govern who may use it and how → privacy.

sections.title: AI Verification Workflow
bullets: Confirm the input data is authorized and safe

sections.title: AI in an IT Scenario
paragraphs: When AI suggests a cause, command, or configuration change, verify it, follow change policy, and protect customer data before acting. AI assists; the technician remains responsible.

sections.title: Objective 4.10 Exam Trap
bullets: Invented information is hallucination; systematically unfair output is bias.
Hallucination is one kind of inaccurate output; accuracy is the broader correctness question.
Public AI is not automatically unsafe; evaluate data, handling, and policy.
Private AI is not automatically secure; controls remain necessary.
Security prevents compromise; privacy governs appropriate collection, use, and sharing.
Data source asks where information came from; accuracy asks whether the result is correct.
AI use is not automatically plagiarism; applicable rules and use determine it.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
sections.callout: Integrate → use appropriately → verify output → protect data.
